editorial.summary: A page-by-page reading of G.I. Joe #60 becomes a discussion of Todd McFarlane and Larry Hama's disputed editorial history, 1980s toy culture, David Choe's uncensored childhood theft and hygiene memories, the mini-comic G.I. Choe, Action Park lore, sexual archetypes and the gap between a comic page and creator-intent speculation. Every idea is preserved while unsafe methods, private-childhood identity, factual uncertainty and explicit speech remain separate layers.

quality.assessment: Complete chronological human read. Dense comics, toy, film and public-name caption damage is repaired where defensible; masked words and uncertain speech remain unresolved. The automatic captions contain no publisher speaker prefixes.

editorial.speaker_policy: The public panel is Jim Rugg, Ed Piskor and David Choe, but participant presence does not identify individual lines. Publish no named turns until held-out acoustic and video validation passes.

connections.relationship: A printed issue becomes the starting point for an unresolved story about authorship, rejection and early career.
Repeated 'fired' language is memorable but remains host framing until creator or production records support it.
Snake Eyes and Storm Shadow organize Choe's memory of an entire creative period.
Toy desire is narrated beside theft, shame and Choe's later jail history rather than as harmless collecting nostalgia.
A complete historical transcript can coexist with suppressing concealment mechanics from snippets and recommendations.
The house ad dates the uploaded program but should not become live commerce.
The panel reads cast expansion as a publishing story driven partly by the toy line.
Nostalgia for realistic toys meets a high-harm claim that requires authoritative evidence.
A specific toy anchors a story whose creative meaning survives without identity-resolving another child.
Choe sees himself in Zanzibar's smell and stealing while acknowledging the humiliation of exclusion.
G.I. Choe links an early commercial-media obsession to Choe's own small-press practice.
Choe places the mini-comic in the same creative universe without establishing a formal sequel or edition.
Page composition prompts a workflow hypothesis that requires scripts, layouts or creator testimony.
A comic's physical exaggeration opens a digression into dangerous-amusement oral history.
The issue is treated as an early-career hinge, but dates and 'first work' claims require primary credits.
Chuckles is read through skate films, television archetypes and action-star style.
Choe explicitly connects female G.I. Joe characters to later attraction while the archive avoids universalizing it.
Anecdotal statue touching is not enough to explain physical wear or a whole culture's behavior.
The hosts' page reading generates plausible editorial theories but not proof of Hama's thoughts.
The panel places G.I. Joe immediately before a better-known Marvel phase, making exact credit chronology valuable.
Michael Golden and Mike Zeck are named as the art language against which this early McFarlane work is read.
The larger helicopter turns remembered desire into more explicit concealment and escape behavior.
The panel ends by proposing direct interviews rather than pretending the episode resolved its central dispute.
